nodes.name: MaxLin2
nodes.statement: In the problem \textsc{MaxLin2}, we are given a system $S$ consisting of $m$ equations in variables $x_1,\ldots ,x_n$, where each equation is $\prod_{i \in I_j}x_i = b_j$ and $x_i,b_j \in \{-1, 1\}$, $j=1,\ldots ,m$. Equation $j$ is assigned a positive integral weight $w_j$ and we wish to find an assignment of values to the variables in order to maximize the total weight of the satisfied equations.
nodes.statement_short: Given a weighted system of product equations over $\{-1,1\}$, find an assignment maximizing the total weight of satisfied equations.

nodes.name: Total weight W and sat(S)
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be the sum of the weights of all equations in $S$ and let ${\rm sat}(S)$ be the maximum total weight of equations that can be satisfied simultaneously.

nodes.name: W/2 is a tight lower bound on sat(S)
nodes.statement: To see that $W/2$ is a tight lower bound on ${\rm sat}(S)$ choose assignments to the variables independently and uniformly at random. Then $W/2$ is the expected weight of satisfied equations (as the probability of each equation being satisfied is $1/2$) and thus $W/2$ is a lower bound; to see the tightness consider a system consisting of pairs of equations of the form $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=-1,\ \prod_{i\in I}x_i=1$ of the same weight, for some non-empty sets $I \subseteq [n]$.
nodes.statement_short: A uniformly random assignment satisfies weight $W/2$ in expectation, and pairs of contradictory equations show the bound is tight.

nodes.name: MaxLin2-AA
nodes.statement: \begin{quote} {\sc MaxLin2-AA}\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Instance:} A system $S$ of equations $\prod_{i \in I_j}x_i = b_j$, where $x_i, b_j \in \{-1,1\}$, $j=1,\ldots ,m$; equation $j$ is assigned a positive integral weight $w_j$, and a nonnegative integer $k$.\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Question:} ${\rm sat}(S)\ge W/2 + k$? \end{quote}
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a weighted system of equations over $\{-1,1\}$ has an assignment satisfying weight at least $W/2+k$.

nodes.name: Max-r-Lin2-AA
nodes.statement: \begin{quote} {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Instance:} A system $S$ of equations $\prod_{i \in I_j}x_i = b_j$, where $x_i, b_j \in \{-1,1\}$, $|I_j|\le r$, $j=1,\ldots ,m$; equation $j$ is assigned a positive integral weight $w_j$, and a nonnegative integer $k$.\\ \nopagebreak \emph{Question:} ${\rm sat}(S)\ge W/2+k$? \end{quote}
nodes.statement_short: MaxLin2-AA restricted to equations with at most $r$ variables.

nodes.name: Håstad's inapproximability of Max-r-Lin2-AA
nodes.statement: H\aa stad \cite{Hastad01} proved that, as a maximization problem, {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} with any fixed $r\ge 3$ (and hence {\sc MaxLin2-AA}) cannot be approximated within $c$ for any $c>1$ unless P$=$NP (that is, the problem is not in APX unless P$=$NP).
assumptions: as a maximization problem, {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} with any fixed $r\ge 3$
conclusions: cannot be approximated within $c$ for any $c>1$ unless P$=$NP

nodes.name: Håstad–Venkatesh approximation algorithm for Max-r-Lin2-AA
nodes.statement: In particular, they proved that for {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} there exist a constant $c>1$ and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, with probability at least 3/4, outputs an assignment with an approximation ratio of at most $c^r\sqrt{m}.$
conclusions: there exist a constant $c>1$ and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, with probability at least 3/4, outputs an assignment with an approximation ratio of at most $c^r\sqrt{m}.$

nodes.name: Complexity of MaxLin2-AA[k] (Mahajan et al.)
nodes.statement: Despite some progress \cite{CroGutJon10,CroGutJonKimRuz10,GutKimSzeYeo11}, the complexity of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] has remained prominently open in the research area of ``parameterizing above guaranteed bounds'' that has attracted much recent attention (cf. \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11,BolSco2002,CroGutJon10,CroGutJonKimRuz10,GutKimSzeYeo11,KimWil,MahajanRamanSikdar09}) and that still poses well-known and longstanding open problems (e.g., how difficult is it to determine if a planar graph has an independent set of size at least $(n/4)+k$?).
nodes.statement_short: The parameterized complexity of MaxLin2-AA[k] was a prominent open problem in parameterizing above guaranteed bounds.

nodes.name: MaxLin2-AA[k]
nodes.statement: We will denote this parameterized problem by {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$].

nodes.name: Max-r-Lin2-AA[k] and Max-r-Lin2-AA[k,r]
nodes.statement: One can parameterize {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} by $k$ for any fixed $r$ (denoted by {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$]) or by both $k$ and $r$ (denoted by {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$])\footnote{While in the preceding literature only {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] was considered, we introduce and study {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$] in the spirit of Multivariate Algorithmics as outlined by Fellows \cite{FelIWOCA} and Niedermeier \cite{Niedermeier10}.}.
nodes.statement_short: Max-r-Lin2-AA parameterized by $k$ for fixed $r$, or by both $k$ and $r$ (the latter introduced here).

nodes.name: Excess
nodes.statement: Define the \emph{excess} for $x^0=(x^0_1,\ldots ,x^0_n)\in \{-1, 1\}^n$ over $S$ to be $$\varepsilon_S(x^0)=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\prod_{i\in I_j}x^0_i,\ \mbox{ where } c_j=w_{j}b_j.$$
nodes.statement_short: The excess of an assignment is $\sum_j c_j\prod_{i\in I_j}x^0_i$ with $c_j=w_jb_j$.

nodes.name: Maximum excess
nodes.statement: The maximum possible value of $\varepsilon_S(x^0)$ is the {\em maximum excess} of $S$.

nodes.name: Pseudo-boolean function
nodes.statement: Note that the excess is a {\em pseudo-boolean function} \cite{BorHam2002}, i.e., a function that maps $\{-1,1\}^n$ to the set of reals.
differentia: maps $\{-1,1\}^n$ to the set of reals

nodes.name: Gutin et al. kernel for Max-r-Lin2-AA[k]
nodes.statement: Gutin et al. \cite{GutKimSzeYeo11} proved that {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$] is fixed-parameter tractable and, moreover, has a kernel with $n\le m = O(k^2)$.
conclusions: {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$] is fixed-parameter tractable
has a kernel with $n\le m = O(k^2)$

nodes.name: Crowston et al. kernel with O(k log k) variables
nodes.statement: This kernel for {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$] was improved by Crowston et al. \cite{CroGutJonKimRuz10}, with respect to the number of variables, to $n = O(k\log k)$.

nodes.name: Kim–Williams linear-variable kernel
nodes.statement: For {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k$], Kim and Williams \cite{KimWil} were the first to obtain a kernel with a linear number of variables, i.e., $n = O(k)$.

nodes.name: Fourier expansion of pseudo-boolean functions
nodes.statement: each function $f:\ \{-1,1\}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ can be uniquely written as \begin{equation} f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i.\end{equation} where ${\cal F}\subseteq \{I:\ \emptyset \neq I\subseteq [n]\}$, $[n]=\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ and $\hat{f}(I)$ are non-zero reals.
assumptions: ${\cal F}\subseteq \{I:\ \emptyset \neq I\subseteq [n]\}$, $[n]=\{1,2,\ldots ,n\}$ and $\hat{f}(I)$ are non-zero reals
conclusions: each function $f:\ \{-1,1\}^n\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ can be uniquely written as
nodes.statement_short: Every function $\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ has a unique multilinear (Fourier) expansion.

nodes.name: Fourier expansion formula
nodes.statement: f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i.
nodes.label: eq1a

nodes.name: Fourier expansion and Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: Formula (\ref{eq1a}) is the Fourier expansion of $f$ and $\hat{f}(I)$ are the Fourier coefficients of $f$.

nodes.name: Degree of a pseudo-boolean function
nodes.statement: The right hand size of (\ref{eq1a}) is a polynomial and the degree $\max \{|I|:\ I\in {\cal F}\}$ of this polynomial will be called the {\em degree} of $f$.

nodes.name: Parameterized problem
nodes.statement: A \emph{parameterized problem} is a subset $L\subseteq \Sigma^* \times \mathbb{N}$ over a finite alphabet $\Sigma$.

nodes.name: Fixed-parameter tractable (FPT)
nodes.statement: $L$ is \emph{fixed-parameter tractable} (FPT, for short) if the membership of an instance $(x,k)$ in $\Sigma^* \times \mathbb{N}$ can be decided in time $f(k)|x|^{O(1)},$ where $f$ is a function of the parameter $k$ only.
nodes.statement_short: $L$ is FPT if membership of $(x,k)$ is decidable in time $f(k)|x|^{O(1)}$.

nodes.name: Class XP
nodes.statement: When the decision time is replaced by the much more powerful $|x|^{O(f(k))},$ we obtain the class XP, where each problem is polynomial-time solvable for any fixed value of $k.$

nodes.name: W-hierarchy between FPT and XP
nodes.statement: There is an infinite number of parameterized complexity classes between FPT and XP (for each integer $t\ge 1$, there is a class W[$t$]) and they form the following tower: $FPT \subseteq W[1] \subseteq W[2] \subseteq \cdots \subseteq XP.$

nodes.name: Bikernelization
nodes.statement: Given a pair $L,L'$ of parameterized problems, a \emph{bikernelization from $L$ to $L'$} is a polynomial-time algorithm that maps an instance $(x,k)$ to an instance $(x',k')$ (the \emph{bikernel}) such that (i)~$(x,k)\in L$ if and only if $(x',k')\in L'$, (ii)~ $k'\leq f(k)$, and (iii)~$|x'|\leq g(k)$ for some functions $f$ and $g$.
differentia: (i)~$(x,k)\in L$ if and only if $(x',k')\in L'$
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-time map from instances of $L$ to equivalent instances of $L'$ whose parameter and size are bounded by functions of $k$.

nodes.name: Size of a bikernel
nodes.statement: The function $g(k)$ is called the {\em size} of the bikernel.

nodes.name: FPT iff bikernelization
nodes.statement: The notion of a bikernelization was introduced in \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11}, where it was observed that a parameterized problem $L$ is fixed-parameter tractable if and only if it is decidable and admits a bikernelization from itself to a parameterized problem $L'$.
conclusions: a parameterized problem $L$ is fixed-parameter tractable if and only if it is decidable and admits a bikernelization from itself to a parameterized problem $L'$

nodes.name: Kernelization and kernel
nodes.statement: A {\em kernelization} of a parameterized problem $L$ is simply a bikernelization from $L$ to itself; the bikernel is the {\em kernel}, and $g(k)$ is the {\em size} of the kernel.

nodes.name: Reducing several parameters to one
nodes.statement: The case of several parameters $k_1,\ldots ,k_t$ can be reduced to the one parameter case by setting $k=k_1+\cdots +k_t,$ see, e.g., \cite{DLS09}.

nodes.name: MaxLin2-AA answer via maximum excess
nodes.statement: Observe that the answer to {\sc MaxLin2-AA} is {\sc Yes} if and only if the maximum excess is at least $2k$.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: MaxLin2-AA is a Yes-instance iff the maximum excess is at least $2k$.
nodes.label: MaxLinExcess

nodes.name: Excess and pseudo-boolean functions are equivalent
nodes.statement: The excess $\varepsilon_S(x)$ is a pseudo-boolean function and its Fourier expression is $\varepsilon_S(x)=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\prod_{i\in I_j}x_i$. Moreover, observe that every pseudo-boolean function $f(x)=\sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i$ (where $\hat{f}(\emptyset)=0$) is the excess over the system $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=b_I$, $I\in {\cal F}$, where $b_I=1$ if $\hat{f}(I)>0$ and $b_I=-1$ if $\hat{f}(I)<0$, with weights $|\hat{f}(I)|.$ Thus, studying the maximum excess over a {\sc MaxLin2-AA}-system (with real weights) is equivalent to studying the maximum of a pseudo-boolean function.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Every pseudo-boolean function with zero constant term is the excess of a weighted system with signs and weights from its Fourier coefficients.
nodes.label: PseudoBExcess

nodes.name: Reduction Rule 1
nodes.statement: If we have, for a subset $I$ of $[n]$, an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I'$ with weight $w_I'$, and an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I''$ with weight $w_I''$, then we replace this pair by one of these equations with weight $w_I'+w_I''$ if $b_I'=b_I''$ and, otherwise, by the equation whose weight is bigger, modifying its new weight to be the difference of the two old ones. If the resulting weight is~0, we delete the equation from the system.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Merge two equations with the same left-hand side into one, adding or subtracting weights; delete it if the weight is 0.
input: for a subset $I$ of $[n]$, an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I'$ with weight $w_I'$, and an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I''$ with weight $w_I''$
nodes.label: rule1

nodes.name: Merge equal left-hand sides
nodes.statement: If we have, for a subset $I$ of $[n]$, an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I'$ with weight $w_I'$, and an equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b_I''$ with weight $w_I''$, then we replace this pair by one of these equations with weight $w_I'+w_I''$ if $b_I'=b_I''$ and, otherwise, by the equation whose weight is bigger, modifying its new weight to be the difference of the two old ones.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Replace the pair by one equation with summed or differenced weight.

nodes.name: Delete zero-weight equation
nodes.statement: If the resulting weight is~0, we delete the equation from the system.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Remove an equation whose weight became 0.

nodes.name: Reduction Rule 2
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be the matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ corresponding to the set of equations in $S$, such that $a_{ji} = 1$ if $i \in I_j$ and $0$, otherwise. Let $t={\rm rank} A$ and suppose columns $a^{i_1},\ldots ,a^{i_t}$ of $A$ are linearly independent. Then delete all variables not in $\{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ from the equations of $S$.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Keep only the variables of a maximal set of linearly independent columns of the incidence matrix $A$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
nodes.label: rulerank

nodes.name: Build matrix A
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be the matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ corresponding to the set of equations in $S$, such that $a_{ji} = 1$ if $i \in I_j$ and $0$, otherwise.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Form the equation-variable incidence matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$.

nodes.name: Choose independent columns
nodes.statement: Let $t={\rm rank} A$ and suppose columns $a^{i_1},\ldots ,a^{i_t}$ of $A$ are linearly independent.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Pick $t=\mathrm{rank}A$ linearly independent columns.

nodes.name: Delete other variables
nodes.statement: Then delete all variables not in $\{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ from the equations of $S$.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: Remove all variables outside the chosen columns.

nodes.name: Reduction rules preserve maximum excess
nodes.statement: \cite{GutKimSzeYeo11} Let $S'$ be obtained from $S$ by Rule~\ref{rule1} or \ref{rulerank}. Then the maximum excess of $S'$ is equal to the maximum excess of $S$. Moreover, $S'$ can be obtained from $S$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $m$.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
assumptions: Let $S'$ be obtained from $S$ by Rule~\ref{rule1} or \ref{rulerank}.
conclusions: Then the maximum excess of $S'$ is equal to the maximum excess of $S$.
Moreover, $S'$ can be obtained from $S$ in time polynomial in $n$ and $m$.
nodes.label: lem:SS'

nodes.name: Irreducible system
nodes.statement: If we cannot change a weighted system $S$ using Rules~\ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, we call it {\em irreducible}.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
differentia: we cannot change a weighted system $S$ using Rules~\ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}

nodes.name: Rule 1 then Rule 2 yields an irreducible system
nodes.statement: Let $S'$ be a system obtained from $S$ by first applying Rule~\ref{rule1} as long as possible and then Rule \ref{rulerank} as long as possible. Then $S'$ is irreducible.
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
assumptions: Let $S'$ be a system obtained from $S$ by first applying Rule~\ref{rule1} as long as possible and then Rule \ref{rulerank} as long as possible.
conclusions: Then $S'$ is irreducible.
nodes.label: lem:irred

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (irreducibility after Rules 1, 2)
nodes.statement: Let $S^*$ denote the system obtained from $S$ by applying Rule~\ref{rule1} as long as possible. Without loss of generality, assume that $x_1\not\in \{x_{i_1},\ldots ,x_{i_t}\}$ (see the description of Rule \ref{rulerank}) and thus Rule \ref{rulerank} removes $x_1$ from $S^*$. To prove the lemma it suffices to show that after $x_1$ removal no pair of equations has the same left hand side. Suppose that there is a pair of equations in $S^*$ which has the same left hand side after $x_1$ removal; let $\prod_{i \in I'} x_i =b'$ and $\prod_{i \in I''} x_i =b''$ be such equations and let $I'=I''\cup \{1\}$. Then the entries of the first column of $A$, $a^1$, corresponding to the pair of equations are 1 and 0, but in all the other columns of $A$ the entries corresponding to the the pair of equations are either 1,1 or 0,0. Thus, $a^1$ is independent from all the other columns of $A$, a contradiction.\qed
nodes.section: 2 Maximum Excess, Irreducible Systems and Algorithm $\cal H$
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: two equations with equal left-hand sides after removing $x_1$ would make column $a^1$ independent of the others.

nodes.name: Set up S* and WLOG

nodes.name: Algorithm H

nodes.name: Proof of the n^{2k} algorithm
nodes.statement: Suppose we have an instance $\cal L$ of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] that is reduced by Rules \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, and that the maximum excess of $\cal L$ is at least $2k$. Let $A$ be the matrix introduced in Rule \ref{rulerank}. Pick $n$ equations $e_1,\ldots , e_n$ such that their rows in $A$ are linearly independent. Any assignment must either satisfy one of these equations, or falsify them all. We can check, in time $(nm)^{O(1)}$, what happens if they are all falsified, as fixing the values of these $n$ equations fixes the values of all the others. If falsifying all the equations does not lead to an excess of at least $2k$, then any assignment of values to $x_1,\ldots ,x_n$ that leads to excess at least $2k$ must satisfy at least one of $e_1, \ldots ,e_n$. Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemExcess}, algorithm $\cal H$ can mark one of these equations and achieve an excess of at least $2k$. This gives us the following depth-bounded search tree. At each node $N$ of the tree, reduce the system by Rules \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank}, and let $n'$ be the number of variables in the reduced system. Then find $n'$ equations $e_1,\ldots ,e_{n'}$ corresponding to linearly independent vectors. Find an assignment of values to $x_1,\ldots ,x_{n'}$ that falsifies all of $e_1,\ldots , e_{n'}$. Check whether this assignment achieves excess of at least $2k-w^*$, where $w^*$ is total weight of equations marked by $\cal H$ in all predecessors of $N$. If it does, then return the assignment and stop the algorithm. Otherwise, split into $n'$ branches. In the $i$'th branch, run an iteration of $\cal H$ marking equation $e_i$. Then repeat this algorithm for each new node. Whenever the total weight of marked equations is at least $2k,$ return the suitable assignment. Clearly, the algorithm will terminate without an assignment if the maximum excess of $\cal L$ is less than $2k.$ All the operations at each node take time $(nm)^{O(1)}$, and there are less than $n^{2k+1}$ nodes in the search tree. Therefore this algorithm takes time $n^{2k}(nm)^{O(1)}$.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Depth-bounded search tree: either falsifying $n$ independent equations already works, or some must be satisfied and is marked by Algorithm H. The tree has depth at most $2k$ and branching $n$.

nodes.name: MaxLin2-AA[k] kernel with O(k^2 log k) variables
nodes.statement: The problem {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] has a kernel with at most $O(k^2\log k)$ variables.
conclusions: The problem {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] has a kernel with at most $O(k^2\log k)$ variables.
nodes.label: thm:main

nodes.name: Proof of the O(k^2 log k) kernel
nodes.statement: Let $\cal L$ be an instance of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] and let $S$ be the system of $\cal L$ with $m$ equations and $n$ variables. We may assume that $S$ is irreducible. Let the parameter $k$ be an arbitrary positive integer. If $m<2k$ then $n<2k=O(k^2\log k)$. If $2k\le m\le 2^{n/(2k-1)}-2$ then, by Theorem \ref{thm:ing2}, the answer to $\cal L$ is {\sc yes} and the corresponding assignment can be found in polynomial time. If $m\ge n^{2k}$ then, by Theorem \ref{thm:ing1}, we can solve $\cal L$ in polynomial time. Finally we consider the case $2^{n/(2k-1)}-1 \le m \le n^{2k}-1$. Hence, $n^{2k}\ge 2^{n/(2k-1)}.$ Therefore, $4k^2\ge 2+n/\log n \ge \sqrt{n}$ and $n\le (2k)^4$. Hence, $n\le 4k^2\log n\le 4k^2\log(16k^4)=O(k^2\log k).$ Since $S$ is irreducible, $m<2^n$ and thus we have obtained the desired kernel. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on $m$: small $m$, the Crowston et al. range, and $m\ge n^{2k}$ are solved directly; the remaining range forces $n=O(k^2\log k)$.

nodes.name: Sum-free subset lemma
nodes.statement: Let $M$ be a set of vectors in $\mathbb{F}^n_2$ such that $M$ contains a basis of $\mathbb{F}^n_2.$ Suppose that each vector of $M$ contains at most $r$ non-zero coordinates. If $k\ge 1$ is an integer and $n \ge r(k-1)+1$, then in time $|M|^{O(1)}$, we can find a subset $K$ of $M$ of $k$ vectors such that $K$ is $M$-sum-free.

nodes.name: Proof of the sum-free subset lemma
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{1} = (1, \ldots, 1)$ be the vector in $\mathbb{F}^n_2$ in which every coordinate is $1$. Note that $\mathbf{1}\not\in M.$ By our assumption $M$ contains a basis of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and we may find such a basis in polynomial time (using Gaussian elimination, see above). We may write $\mathbf{1}$ as a sum of some vectors of this basis $B$. This implies that $\mathbf{1}$ can be expressed as follows: $\mathbf{1} = v_1 + v_2 + \cdots + v_s$, where $\{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}\subseteq B$ and $v_1, \ldots, v_s$ are linearly independent, and we can find such an expression in polynomial time. For each $v \in M \backslash \{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$, consider the set $S_v=\{v, v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$. In polynomial time, we may check whether $S_v$ is linearly independent. Consider two cases: \begin{description} \item[Case 1:] $S_v$ is linearly independent for each $v \in M \backslash \{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$. Then $\{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$ is $M$-sum-free (here we also use the fact that $\{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$ is linearly independent). Since each $v_i$ has at most $r$ positive coordinates, we have $sr\ge n> r(k-1)$. Hence, $s>k-1$ implying that $s\ge k$. Thus, $\{v_1, \ldots, v_k\}$ is the required set $K$. \item[Case 2:] $S_v$ is linearly dependent for some $v\in M \backslash \{v_1, \ldots, v_s\}$. Then we can find (in polynomial time) $I \subseteq [s]$ such that $v=\sum_{i \in I} v_i$. Thus, we have a shorter expression for $\mathbf{1}$: $\mathbf{1} = v'_1 + v'_2 + \cdots + v'_{s'}$, where $\{v'_1, \ldots , v'_{s'}\}=\{v\} \cup \{ v_i : i \notin I\}$. Note that $\{v'_1, \ldots , v'_{s'}\}$ is linearly independent. \end{description} Since $s\le n$ and Case 2 produces a shorter expression for $\mathbf{1}$, after at most $n$ iterations of Case 2 we will arrive at Case 1. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Write the all-ones vector as a sum of basis vectors and repeatedly shorten the expression; when no shortening exists the summands are $M$-sum-free and number at least $k$.

nodes.name: Proof of the maximum excess lower bound
nodes.statement: Consider a set $M$ of vectors in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ corresponding to equations in $S$ as follows: for each equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b$ in $S$, define a vector $v=(v_1,\ldots ,v_{n})\in M$, where $v_i=1$ if $i\in I$ and $v_i=0$, otherwise. As $S$ is reduced by Rule \ref{rulerank} we have that $M$ contains a basis for $\mathbb{F}^n_2$, and each vector contains at most $r$ non-zero coordinates and $n\ge (k-1)r+1$. Therefore, using Lemma \ref{thmKcon} we can find an $M$-sum-free set $K$ of $k$ vectors. Let $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ be the corresponding set of equations. Run Algorithm $\cal H$, choosing at Step 1 an equation of $S$ from $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ each time, and let $S'$ be the resulting system. Algorithm $\cal H$ will run for $k$ iterations of the while loop as no equation from $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ will be deleted before it has been marked. Indeed, suppose that this is not true. Then for some $e_{j_l}$ and some other equation $e$ in $S$, after applying Algorithm $\cal H$ for at most $l-1$ iterations $e_{j_l}$ and $e$ contain the same variables. Thus, there are vectors $v_j\in K$ and $v\in M$ and a pair of nonintersecting subsets $K'$ and $K''$ of $K\setminus \{v,v_j\}$ such that $v_j+\sum_{u\in K'}u=v+\sum_{u\in K''}u$. Thus, $v=v_j+\sum_{u\in K'\cup K''}u$, a contradiction with the definition of $K.$ Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemExcess}, we are done. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Take an $M$-sum-free set of $k$ equation vectors (sum-free lemma) and run Algorithm H on them; sum-freeness ensures none is deleted before being marked.

nodes.name: Vectors of equations and sum-free set
nodes.statement: Consider a set $M$ of vectors in $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ corresponding to equations in $S$ as follows: for each equation $\prod_{i \in I} x_i =b$ in $S$, define a vector $v=(v_1,\ldots ,v_{n})\in M$, where $v_i=1$ if $i\in I$ and $v_i=0$, otherwise. As $S$ is reduced by Rule \ref{rulerank} we have that $M$ contains a basis for $\mathbb{F}^n_2$, and each vector contains at most $r$ non-zero coordinates and $n\ge (k-1)r+1$. Therefore, using Lemma \ref{thmKcon} we can find an $M$-sum-free set $K$ of $k$ vectors.
nodes.statement_short: Associate a 0/1 vector with each equation; the sum-free lemma gives $K$ with $|K|=k$.

nodes.name: Run Algorithm H on K
nodes.statement: Let $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ be the corresponding set of equations. Run Algorithm $\cal H$, choosing at Step 1 an equation of $S$ from $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ each time, and let $S'$ be the resulting system.
nodes.statement_short: Run H choosing equations from $K$ at each step.

nodes.name: H runs k iterations
nodes.statement: Algorithm $\cal H$ will run for $k$ iterations of the while loop as no equation from $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ will be deleted before it has been marked. Indeed, suppose that this is not true. Then for some $e_{j_l}$ and some other equation $e$ in $S$, after applying Algorithm $\cal H$ for at most $l-1$ iterations $e_{j_l}$ and $e$ contain the same variables. Thus, there are vectors $v_j\in K$ and $v\in M$ and a pair of nonintersecting subsets $K'$ and $K''$ of $K\setminus \{v,v_j\}$ such that $v_j+\sum_{u\in K'}u=v+\sum_{u\in K''}u$. Thus, $v=v_j+\sum_{u\in K'\cup K''}u$, a contradiction with the definition of $K.$
nodes.statement_short: Claim: no chosen equation is deleted before being marked, so H runs $k$ iterations.

nodes.name: Claim statement
nodes.statement: Algorithm $\cal H$ will run for $k$ iterations of the while loop as no equation from $\{e_{j_1}, \ldots, e_{j_k}\}$ will be deleted before it has been marked.
nodes.statement_short: State that H performs $k$ iterations.

nodes.name: Suppose otherwise
nodes.statement: Indeed, suppose that this is not true. Then for some $e_{j_l}$ and some other equation $e$ in $S$, after applying Algorithm $\cal H$ for at most $l-1$ iterations $e_{j_l}$ and $e$ contain the same variables.
nodes.statement_short: Assume some $e_{j_l}$ coincides with another equation early.

nodes.name: Contradict sum-freeness
nodes.statement: Thus, there are vectors $v_j\in K$ and $v\in M$ and a pair of nonintersecting subsets $K'$ and $K''$ of $K\setminus \{v,v_j\}$ such that $v_j+\sum_{u\in K'}u=v+\sum_{u\in K''}u$. Thus, $v=v_j+\sum_{u\in K'\cup K''}u$, a contradiction with the definition of $K.$
nodes.statement_short: This expresses $v$ as a sum of vectors of $K$, contradicting sum-freeness.

nodes.name: Conclude by excess lemma
nodes.statement: Thus, by Lemma \ref{lemExcess}, we are done. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Marked weight at least $k\,w_{\min}$ gives the excess bound.

nodes.name: Sharpness of n >= r(k-1)+1
nodes.statement: To see that the inequality $n \ge r(k-1)+1$ in the theorem is best possible assume that $n=r(k-1)$ and consider a partition of $[n]$ into $k-1$ subsets $N_1,\ldots ,N_{k-1}$, each of size $r.$ Let $S$ be the system consisting of subsystems $S_i$, $i\in [k-1],$ such that a subsystem $S_i$ is comprised of equations $\prod_{i \in I} x_i=-1$ of weight 1 for every $I$ such that $\emptyset \neq I\subseteq N_i$. Now assume without loss of generality that $N_i=[r]$. Observe that the assignment $(x_1,\ldots ,x_r)=(1,\ldots ,1)$ falsifies all equations of $S_i$ but by setting $x_j=-1$ for any $j\in [r]$ we satisfy the equation $x_j=-1$ and turn the remaining equations into pairs of the form $\prod_{i \in I} x_i=-1$ and $\prod_{i \in I} x_i=1$. Thus, the maximum excess of $S_i$ is 1 and the maximum excess of $S$ is $k-1$.
nodes.statement_short: With $n=r(k-1)$, disjoint blocks of all-$(-1)$ equations show maximum excess only $k-1$.
nodes.label: rem:sharp2

nodes.name: Real weights
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that Theorem \ref{lemYes} holds when the weights of equations in $S$ are real numbers, not necessarily integers.
nodes.statement_short: The excess lower bound also holds for real (non-integral) weights.
nodes.label: rem:reals

nodes.name: Max-r-Lin2-AA[k,r] kernel with (2k-1)r variables
nodes.statement: The problem {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$] has a kernel with at most $(2k-1)r$ variables.
conclusions: The problem {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$] has a kernel with at most $(2k-1)r$ variables.
nodes.label: thLinAAkr

nodes.name: Proof of the (2k-1)r kernel
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be the system of an instance of {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$]. After applying Rules \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank} to $T$ as long as possible, we obtain a new system $S$ which is irreducible. Let $n$ be the number of variables in $S$ and observe that the number of variables in an equation in $S$ is bounded by $r$ (as in $T$). If $n \ge (2k-1)r+1$, then, by Theorem \ref{lemYes} and Remark \ref{MaxLinExcess}, $S$ is a {\sc Yes}-instance of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k,r$] and, hence, by Lemma \ref{lem:SS'}, $S$ and $T$ are both {\sc Yes}-instances of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k,r$]. Otherwise $n \le (2k-1)r$ and we have the required kernel. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an irreducible system; if it has at least $(2k-1)r+1$ variables the excess bound answers Yes, otherwise it is the kernel.

nodes.name: Reduce to irreducible S
nodes.statement: Let $T$ be the system of an instance of {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}[$k,r$]. After applying Rules \ref{rule1} and \ref{rulerank} to $T$ as long as possible, we obtain a new system $S$ which is irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Rules 1 and 2 exhaustively to get irreducible $S$.

nodes.name: Many variables: Yes
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be the number of variables in $S$ and observe that the number of variables in an equation in $S$ is bounded by $r$ (as in $T$). If $n \ge (2k-1)r+1$, then, by Theorem \ref{lemYes} and Remark \ref{MaxLinExcess}, $S$ is a {\sc Yes}-instance of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k,r$] and, hence, by Lemma \ref{lem:SS'}, $S$ and $T$ are both {\sc Yes}-instances of {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k,r$].
nodes.statement_short: Equations keep at most $r$ variables; with many variables the excess bound gives a Yes-instance.

nodes.name: Few variables: kernel
nodes.statement: Otherwise $n \le (2k-1)r$ and we have the required kernel. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the reduced system is the kernel.

nodes.name: Max-r-Lin2-AA is in APX for m=O(n) and bounded weights
nodes.statement: The maximization problem {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} is in APX if restricted to $m=O(n)$ and the weight of each equation is bounded by a constant.
assumptions: if restricted to $m=O(n)$ and the weight of each equation is bounded by a constant
conclusions: The maximization problem {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA} is in APX

nodes.name: Proof of APX membership
nodes.statement: It follows from Theorem \ref{thLinAAkr} that the answer to {\sc Max-$r$-Lin2-AA}, as a decision problem, is {\sc Yes} as long as $2k\le \lfloor (n+r-1)/r\rfloor.$ This implies approximation ratio at most $W/(2\lfloor (n+r-1)/r\rfloor)$ which is bounded by a constant provided $m=O(n)$ and the weight of each equation is bounded by a constant (then $W=O(n)$). \qed
nodes.statement_short: The kernel bound gives a Yes answer for $2k\le\lfloor(n+r-1)/r\rfloor$, hence a constant approximation ratio.

nodes.name: Max-r-CSP (above average)
nodes.statement: The (parameterized) Boolean Max-$r$-Constraint Satisfaction Problem ({\sc Max-$r$-CSP}) generalizes {\sc MaxLin2-AA}[$k,r$] as follows: We are given a set $\Phi$ of Boolean functions, each involving at most $r$ variables, and a collection ${\cal F}$ of $m$ Boolean functions, each $f \in \cal F$ being a member of $\Phi$, and each acting on some subset of the $n$ Boolean variables $x_1,x_2, \ldots ,x_n$ (each $x_i\in \{-1,1\}$). We are to decide whether there is a truth assignment to the $n$ variables such that the total number of satisfied functions is at least $E+k$, where $E$ is the average value of the number of satisfied functions. The parameters are $k$ and $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether $m$ Boolean constraints of arity at most $r$ admit an assignment satisfying at least $E+k$ of them, $E$ the average.

nodes.name: Bikernel for Max-r-CSP
nodes.statement: Using a bikernelization algorithm described in \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11,CroGutJonKimRuz10} and our new kernel result, it easy to see that {\sc Max-$r$-CSP} with parameters $k$ and $r$ admits a bikernel with at most $(k2^{r+1}-1)r$ variables.
conclusions: {\sc Max-$r$-CSP} with parameters $k$ and $r$ admits a bikernel with at most $(k2^{r+1}-1)r$ variables

nodes.name: Lower bound on the maximum of a pseudo-boolean function
nodes.statement: Let \begin{equation} f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i\end{equation} be a pseudo-boolean function of degree $r$. Then \begin{equation}\max_x f(x)\ge \hat{f}(\emptyset) + \lfloor ({\rm rank} A +r -1)/r\rfloor \cdot \min \{|\hat{f}(I)|: I\in {\cal F}\},\end{equation} where $A$ is a $(0,1)$-matrix with entries $a_{ij}$ such that $a_{ij}=1$ if and only if term $j$ in (\ref{fourier}) contains $x_i.$ One can find an assignment of values to $x$ satisfying (\ref{LBpb1t}) in time $(n|{\cal F}|)^{O(1)}.$
assumptions: be a pseudo-boolean function of degree $r$.
conclusions: One can find an assignment of values to $x$ satisfying (\ref{LBpb1t}) in time $(n|{\cal F}|)^{O(1)}.$
nodes.statement_short: A degree-$r$ pseudo-boolean function attains at least $\hat f(\emptyset)+\lfloor(\mathrm{rank}A+r-1)/r\rfloor\min|\hat f(I)|$, findable in polynomial time.
nodes.label: thm:PBB

nodes.name: Fourier expansion of f
nodes.statement: f(x)=\hat{f}(\emptyset) + \sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i

nodes.name: Proof of the pseudo-boolean lower bound
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} the function $f(x) - \hat{f}(\emptyset) =\sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i$ is the excess over the system $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=b_I$, $I\in {\cal F}$, where $b_I=+1$ if $\hat{f}(I)>0$ and $b_I=-1$ if $\hat{f}(I)<0$, with weights $|\hat{f}(I)|.$ Clearly, Rule \ref{rule1} will not change the system. Using Rule \ref{rulerank} we can replace the system by an equivalent one (by Lemma \ref{lem:SS'}) with ${\rm rank} A$ variables. By Lemma \ref{lem:irred}, the new system is irreducible and we can now apply Theorem \ref{lemYes}. By this theorem, Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} and Remark \ref{rem:reals}, $\max_x f(x)\ge \hat{f}(\emptyset)+k^*\min \{|\hat{f}(I)|: I\in {\cal F}\}$, where $k^*$ is the maximum value of $k$ satisfying ${\rm rank} A\ge (k-1)r+1$. It remains to observe that $k^*=\lfloor ({\rm rank} A +r -1)/r\rfloor$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: View $f-\hat f(\emptyset)$ as an excess, reduce by Rule 2 to $\mathrm{rank}A$ variables, and apply the maximum-excess bound with real weights.

nodes.name: f as an excess
nodes.statement: By Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} the function $f(x) - \hat{f}(\emptyset) =\sum_{I\in {\cal F}}\hat{f}(I)\prod_{i\in I}x_i$ is the excess over the system $\prod_{i\in I}x_i=b_I$, $I\in {\cal F}$, where $b_I=+1$ if $\hat{f}(I)>0$ and $b_I=-1$ if $\hat{f}(I)<0$, with weights $|\hat{f}(I)|.$ Clearly, Rule \ref{rule1} will not change the system.
nodes.statement_short: Interpret $f-\hat f(\emptyset)$ as the excess of a weighted system.

nodes.name: Reduce by Rule 2
nodes.statement: Using Rule \ref{rulerank} we can replace the system by an equivalent one (by Lemma \ref{lem:SS'}) with ${\rm rank} A$ variables.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to ${\rm rank} A$ variables without changing the maximum.

nodes.name: Irreducible; apply theorem
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:irred}, the new system is irreducible and we can now apply Theorem \ref{lemYes}.
nodes.statement_short: The reduced system is irreducible, so the excess bound applies.

nodes.name: Bound with k*
nodes.statement: By this theorem, Remark \ref{PseudoBExcess} and Remark \ref{rem:reals}, $\max_x f(x)\ge \hat{f}(\emptyset)+k^*\min \{|\hat{f}(I)|: I\in {\cal F}\}$, where $k^*$ is the maximum value of $k$ satisfying ${\rm rank} A\ge (k-1)r+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Get $\max f\ge\hat f(\emptyset)+k^*\min|\hat f(I)|$.

nodes.name: Compute k*
nodes.statement: It remains to observe that $k^*=\lfloor ({\rm rank} A +r -1)/r\rfloor$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Compute $k^*=\lfloor(\mathrm{rank}A+r-1)/r\rfloor$.

nodes.name: Incidence matrix
nodes.statement: For a graph $G=(V,E)$, an incidence matrix is a $(0,1)$-matrix with entries $m_{e,v}$, $e\in E$, $v\in V$ such that $m_{e,v}=1$ if and only if $v$ is incident to $e$.
differentia: $m_{e,v}=1$ if and only if $v$ is incident to $e$

nodes.name: Rank of the incidence matrix of a connected graph
nodes.statement: The rank of an incident matrix $M$ of a connected graph equals $|V|-1.$
assumptions: an incident matrix $M$ of a connected graph
conclusions: equals $|V|-1.$
nodes.label: lem:M

nodes.name: Edwards-Erdős bound
nodes.statement: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges. Then $G$ contains a bipartite subgraph with at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges. Such a subgraph can be found in polynomial time.
assumptions: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges.
conclusions: Then $G$ contains a bipartite subgraph with at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges.
Such a subgraph can be found in polynomial time.

nodes.name: New proof of the Edwards-Erdős bound
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Observe that the maximum number of edges in a bipartite subgraph of $G$ equals the maximum number of properly colored edges (i.e., edges whose end-vertices received different colors) over all 2-colorings of $G$. For an edge $e=v_iv_j\in E$ consider the following function $f_e(x)=\frac{1}{2}(1-x_ix_j)$, where $x_i=c(v_i)$ and $x_j=c(v_j)$ and observe that $f_e(x)=1$ if $e$ is properly colored by $c$ and $f_e(x)=0,$ otherwise. Thus, $f(x)=\sum_{e\in E}f_e(x)$ is the number of properly colored edges for $c$. We have $f(x)=\frac{m}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e\in E}x_ix_j$. By Theorem \ref{thm:PBB}, $\max_x f(x)\ge m/2 + \lfloor ({\rm rank} A +2 -1)/2\rfloor/2.$ Observe that matrix $A$ in this bound is an incidence matrix of $G$ and, thus, by Lemma \ref{lem:M} ${\rm rank} A = n-1$. Hence, $\max_x f(x)\ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor \ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ as required. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Count properly colored edges as a degree-2 pseudo-boolean function and apply the pseudo-boolean lower bound with rank of the incidence matrix $n-1$.

nodes.name: Colorings and bipartite subgraphs
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Observe that the maximum number of edges in a bipartite subgraph of $G$ equals the maximum number of properly colored edges (i.e., edges whose end-vertices received different colors) over all 2-colorings of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Max bipartite subgraph equals max number of properly colored edges.

nodes.name: Edge indicator functions
nodes.statement: For an edge $e=v_iv_j\in E$ consider the following function $f_e(x)=\frac{1}{2}(1-x_ix_j)$, where $x_i=c(v_i)$ and $x_j=c(v_j)$ and observe that $f_e(x)=1$ if $e$ is properly colored by $c$ and $f_e(x)=0,$ otherwise. Thus, $f(x)=\sum_{e\in E}f_e(x)$ is the number of properly colored edges for $c$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $f_e=(1-x_ix_j)/2$ and $f=\sum_e f_e$.

nodes.name: Apply pseudo-boolean bound
nodes.statement: We have $f(x)=\frac{m}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{e\in E}x_ix_j$. By Theorem \ref{thm:PBB}, $\max_x f(x)\ge m/2 + \lfloor ({\rm rank} A +2 -1)/2\rfloor/2.$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the pseudo-boolean lower bound with $r=2$.

nodes.name: Rank of incidence matrix
nodes.statement: Observe that matrix $A$ in this bound is an incidence matrix of $G$ and, thus, by Lemma \ref{lem:M} ${\rm rank} A = n-1$.
nodes.statement_short: $A$ is the incidence matrix of $G$, of rank $n-1$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, $\max_x f(x)\ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\lfloor \frac{n}{2} \rfloor \ge \frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ as required. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Simplify to $m/2+(n-1)/4$.

nodes.name: Balanced Subgraph
nodes.statement: This theorem can be extended to the {\sc Balance Subgraph} problem \cite{BocHufTruWah2009}, where we are given a graph $G=(V,E)$ in which each edge is labeled either by $=$ or by $\neq$ and we are asked to find a 2-coloring of $V$ such that the maximum number of edges is satisfied; an edge labeled by $=$ ($\neq$, resp.) is {\em satisfied} if and only if the colors of its end-vertices are the same (different, resp.).
nodes.statement_short: Given a graph with edges labelled $=$ or $\neq$, find a 2-coloring maximizing the number of satisfied edges.

nodes.name: Edwards-Erdős bound for Balanced Subgraph
nodes.statement: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges labeled by either $=$ or $\neq$. There is a 2-coloring of $V$ that satisfies at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges of $G$. Such a 2-coloring can be found in polynomial time.
assumptions: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges labeled by either $=$ or $\neq$.
conclusions: There is a 2-coloring of $V$ that satisfies at least $\frac{m}{2} + \frac{n-1}{4}$ edges of $G$.
Such a 2-coloring can be found in polynomial time.

nodes.name: Proof of the Balanced Subgraph bound
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Let $x_p=c(v_p)$, $p\in [n].$ For an edge $v_iv_j\in E$ we set $s_{ij}=1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $\neq$ and $s_{ij}=-1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $=$. Then the function $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v_iv_j\in E}(1-s_{ij}x_ix_j)$ counts the number of edges satisfied by $c$. The rest of the proof is similar to that in the previous theorem. \qed
nodes.statement_short: As for Edwards-Erdős, with the counting function $\frac12\sum(1-s_{ij}x_ix_j)$.

nodes.name: Colorings as variables
nodes.statement: Let $V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots , v_n\}$ and let $c:\ V\rightarrow \{-1,1\}$ be a 2-coloring of $G$. Let $x_p=c(v_p)$, $p\in [n].$
nodes.statement_short: Encode a 2-coloring by $x_p=c(v_p)$.

nodes.name: Counting function
nodes.statement: For an edge $v_iv_j\in E$ we set $s_{ij}=1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $\neq$ and $s_{ij}=-1$ if $v_iv_j$ is labeled by $=$. Then the function $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{v_iv_j\in E}(1-s_{ij}x_ix_j)$ counts the number of edges satisfied by $c$. The rest of the proof is similar to that in the previous theorem. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Signed counting function, then argue as in the Edwards-Erdős proof.

nodes.name: Edwards-Erdős bound parameterized above tight bound
nodes.statement: Another question of Mahajan et al. \cite{MahajanRamanSikdar09} remains open: what is the parameterized complexity of deciding whether a connected graph on $n$ vertices and $m$ edges has a bipartite subgraph with at least $m/2+(n-1)/4 + k$ edges, where $k$ is the parameter.
nodes.statement_short: Parameterized complexity of deciding whether a connected graph has a bipartite subgraph with $m/2+(n-1)/4+k$ edges.

nodes.name: Kernel is not polynomial
nodes.statement: The kernel obtained in Theorem \ref{thm:main} is not of polynomial size as it is not polynomial in $m$.

nodes.name: Polynomial kernel for MaxLin2-AA[k]
nodes.statement: The existence of a polynomial-size kernel for \textsc{MaxLin2-AA}[$k$] remains an open problem.

nodes.name: Structural characterization of irreducible systems with small excess
nodes.statement: Perhaps the kernel obtained in Theorem \ref{thm:main} or the algorithm of Corollary \ref{cor1} can be improved if we find a structural characterization of irreducible systems for which the maximum excess is less than $2k.$ Such a characterization can be of interest by itself.

nodes.name: MaxSat-AA[k]
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a CNF formula with clauses $C_1,\ldots ,C_m$ of sizes $r_1,\ldots ,r_m$. Since the probability of $C_i$ being satisfied by a random assignment is $1-2^{-r_i}$, the expected (average) number of satisfied clauses is $E=\sum_{i=1}^m(1-2^{-r_i}).$ It is natural to consider the following parameterized problem {\sc MaxSat-AA}[$k$]: decide whether there is a truth assignment that satisfies at least $E+k$ clauses.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a CNF formula has an assignment satisfying at least $E+k$ clauses, $E$ the expected number.

nodes.name: Max-r-Sat-AA[k]
nodes.statement: When there is a constant $r$ such that $|C_i|\le r$ for each $i=1,\ldots ,m$, {\sc MaxSat-AA}[$k$] is denoted by {\sc Max-$r$-Sat-AA}[$k$].

nodes.name: Max-r-Sat-AA[k] is fixed-parameter tractable
nodes.statement: Mahajan et al. \cite{MahajanRamanSikdar09} asked what is the complexity of {\sc Max-$r$-Sat-AA}[$k$] and Alon et al. \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11} proved that it is fixed-parameter tractable \cite{AloGutKimSzeYeo11}.
conclusions: it is fixed-parameter tractable

nodes.name: Complexity of MaxSat-AA[k]
nodes.statement: It would be interesting to determine the complexity of {\sc MaxSat-AA}[$k$].
